newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWEDEN'S STORA GAINS AS RESULTS BEAT EXPECTATIONS.
newsitem.headline: SWEDEN'S STORA GAINS AS RESULTS BEAT EXPECTATIONS.

text.p: Swedish forestry group Stora on Thursday reported better than expected first quarter earnings and its shares rose slightly.
Stora reported a 54 percent fall in first quarter profit after financial items to 560 million crowns ($73.1 million), compared with market expectations of a fall to 429 million crowns.
The group said in a statement of results that lower prices had a negative impact of 1.7 billion crowns although currency fluctuations improved earnings by 100 million crowns.
"The strong economic trend in the U.S. continues. In Europe there are signs of a recovery, with the strong US exchange rate having a positive effect," the company said.

Stora shares were boosted by the results, standing three crowns higher in early afternoon trade at 102 crowns although sector analysts said they were unlikely to change their 1997 profit forecast of 2.37 billion crowns on the back of the result.
One analyst said the better-than-expected figures meant the market could be more comfortable with its full-year expectations of Stora in the highly cyclical forestry market.
"I am not going to change anything," one analyst said.
Stora said the market for sawn timber, paper and board improved compared with the same period in 1996, part of which was due to customer inventory reductions in 1996.
It said the order backlog for most of its products was from three to five weeks.
The group said that deliveries of its pulp, paper and board rose by nine percent to 1.64 million tonnes with delivery levels unchanged versus the final quarter of last year.
It said the average sales prices for paper and board products were a lot lower, down by 17 percent compared with the first quarter of 1996 and down two percent versus the last quarter of 1996.
Prices for printing papers and packaging were about eight percent lower while board and fine paper prices rose slightly. The price trend for sawn timber was also positive, it added.
The group said it generated earnings in the interest rate and currency markets and in share-related instruments.
It said a slump in earnings in its printing papers business was due to reduced prices while earnings growth in technical papers was due to price rises in late 1996 and February 1997.
Fine papers saw income rise due to higher volumes and improved margins while board and packaging paper saw a fall due to test runs of new products and trimming in of new machines.
In the base products division, power profits rose, partly due to increased hydropower production while its forest division also gained due to lower felling costs and a rise in volumes.
The pulp business saw a larger loss, hit by persistently high inventory levels.
